data.title: Eastern Christian Apocalyptic in the Early Muslim Period: Pseudo-Methodius and Pseudo-Athanasius
data.abstractNote: The apocalyptic writings produced in the Christian East after the Muslim invasions are only partially known to scholars and little studied. The present dissertation edits two such writings, both from the Umayyad period. The Syriac Apocalypse of Pseudo-Methodius (chapter I), from the late VII century, is here edited for the first time from the text in MS Vat. Syr. 58. The text, which is not well preserved in the MS, is improved through a systematic comparison with the Greek and Latin versions of the work, and through recourse to other Syriac sources. An English version, with explanatory notes, accompanies the edition. Chapter II reedits a fragmentary Syriac apocalypse which was considered by its first editor to be the original form of the Syriac Pseudo- Methodius, but which may now be seen a late medieval reworking, probably from the Mongol period. Chapter III edits, also for the first time, the Sahidic Apocalypse of Pseudo-Athanasius, from MS Pierpont Morgan M 602 and the fragment from the Cairo Museum no. 9299, together with the Arabic version of it, based on MS Mingana Syr. 461 and MS Borgia Ar. 200. This Arabic version helps to fill the numerous lacunae in the Coptic text. The work is probably from the first decades of the VIII century. As in chapters I and II, English versions and explanatory notes are provided. These texts afford the scholar an insight into the earliest Christian reaction to the conquering Muslims.

data.title: Histoire de Mār Abba, catholicos de l’Orient. Martyres de Mār Grigor, général en chef du roi Khusro I<sup>er</sup> et de Mār Yazd-panāh, juge et gouverneur
data.abstractNote: The reign of Khusro I (531-579) was a key-period for the history of the Sasanian Empire. Nevertheless, sporadic persecutions of Christians converted from Zoroastrianism are attested. Among these martyrs, there were famous people of civil society such as Grigor Piran-Gusnasp, general-in-chief of the king’s armies, Yazd-panah, a high dignitary and judge, and ‘Awira, a courtier. The most famous was the Catholicos Mar Abba (540-552), who reunified the Church of the East after nearly twenty-five years of schism; canonist and exegete, he also restored ecclesiastical discipline which had been significantly weakened since 484. He is known to have been involved in Mazdeo-Christian controversies and polemical debates with West-Syrian Christians. These narratives written by contemporaries to the events are the only East-Syrian hagiographies of that time in Syriac; they provide valuable informations regarding socio-religious and political situation of the sixth century Orient. A critical edition based on manuscripts from the London, Berlin and Vatican Libraries, including a translation in French with a commentary, is presented for the first time.
